rationale: Official PubMed and Springer article page identify Rahbardar and Hosseinzadeh, published online 2020-07-28, DOI 10.1007/s00210-020-01935-w. The author abstract describes a narrative review of isolated rosmarinic acid, notes it occurs in rosemary, and lists depression among reviewed disorder domains; it reports no fresh rosemary intervention or depressive-severity estimate. Springer exposes the abstract, figures and references but states the article is subscription content; full body not recovered, so exact claim fit remains pending.

Full original protocol (Fielding et al., published online 2011-08-08; issue Nov 2011; DOI 10.1093/gerona/glr123) identifies LIFE, an older-adult trial of supervised physical activity versus successful-aging education. It excludes Parkinson disease (Table 1); neither arm uses lemon balm, and depressive symptoms are not a measured endpoint. Depression appears only as background rationale (Introduction). The frozen brewed-herb exposure and depression-severity endpoint do not match.

Full original protocol (DOI 10.1093/gerona/glr123) excludes Parkinson disease (Table 1), tests physical activity versus health education, and names no millet. Pain severity is not an outcome. The sole body mention of pain is chest pain as one possible safety exclusion during the baseline 400-m walk (Table 1), not symptom measurement. Neither exposure nor endpoint matches boiled millet/pain severity.

Full original Phase 1 report (Kakkar et al., DOI 10.1002/jcph.468; 2015) describes healthy adult men receiving SMT C1100, not refined corn oil. The clinical formulation was an aqueous microfluidized suspension; corn oil appears only as an earlier preclinical toxicology formulation/comparator. The 200 mg/kg twice-daily arm lists constipation among adverse events (Results/Safety), without counts or severity scale. This is non-PD, unrelated-drug symptom context and not an oil effect.

Full original Phase 1 report (DOI 10.1002/jcph.468; 2015) is an unrelated SMT C1100 drug study in healthy adult men; clinical dosing used an aqueous suspension, not corn oil. The report lists tiredness in the 100 mg/kg twice-daily arm as an adverse event, without counts or a fatigue-severity outcome. Fatigue testing appears only in cited mdx-mouse preclinical work in the Discussion, not as a human clinical outcome. No refined corn-oil effect was tested.
